title: What Will Indonesia Do With Its New Aircraft Carrier?
gist: Indonesia has acquired the former Italian carrier Giuseppe Garibaldi, now KRI Sriwijaya, joining a growing club of Western Pacific carrier operators. Robert Farley argues its value depends on how much Indonesia invests in maintaining the ship and its air wing, noting it is smaller than Australian, Indian, Chinese and Japanese flat-decks and comparable to Thailand's Chakri Naruebet.

insights.claim: Indonesia acquired KRI Sriwijaya, a small aircraft carrier formerly operated by the Italian Navy as the Giuseppe Garibaldi, prompting questions about the strategic reasoning behind the purchase.
insights.so_what: Second-hand carrier transfers are an emerging route for mid-sized navies to gain power-projection capability without new-build costs.
insights.locator: Febry Triantama has asked difficult questions
insights.speaker: Robert Farley

insights.claim: The future of KRI Sriwijaya, and of the Indonesian Navy, depends largely on how much Indonesia invests in maintaining and optimizing the vessel and its air wing.
insights.so_what: Follow-on spending on aircraft and sustainment, not the hull purchase, will determine whether the carrier becomes a real capability; watch Indonesian procurement of carrier-capable aircraft.
insights.quote: Much regarding the future of the carrier (and the future of the Indonesian Navy) depends on how much Indonesia invests in maintaining and optimizing the vessel and its air wing.
insights.locator: Febry Triantama has asked difficult questions
insights.speaker: Robert Farley

insights.claim: Indonesia joins a growing club of Western Pacific navies operating aircraft carriers: Australia, India, China and Japan have all built or acquired flat-decked aircraft-carrying warships in recent years.
insights.so_what: Regional proliferation of flat-decks reflects a naval arms buildup in the Indo-Pacific, supporting demand for naval aviation and shipbuilding.
insights.speaker: Robert Farley

insights.claim: Most other regional carriers are considerably larger than KRI Sriwijaya and can carry more and more varied aircraft and operate farther from base.
insights.so_what: Sriwijaya will be a limited capability relative to peers, better suited to regional roles than high-end power projection.
insights.speaker: Robert Farley

insights.claim: Thailand joined the carrier club in the 1990s with the Spanish-designed Chakri Naruebet, similar in size to KRI Sriwijaya, offering a comparable precedent for a Southeast Asian small-carrier operator.
insights.so_what: Thailand's experience is a reference case for whether a small Southeast Asian carrier delivers lasting capability or becomes underused.
insights.speaker: Robert Farley
